newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Albanian violence reaches northern borders.
newsitem.headline: Albanian violence reaches northern borders.

text.p: Albania's violence reached its northern borders on Thursday when guards engaged Macedonian frontier police in a fire-fight.
Yugoslavia, expressing alarm at the "deep destabilisation" of its neighbour, closed its border and raised combat readiness of its troops.
The fire-fight, in which no one was injured, occurred after a watchtower on the Albanian side of the border with Macedonia was seized by local rebel forces, the Defence Ministry in Skopje said.
Seven Albanian border policemen then tried to cross the border at Kjafasan and opened fire at Macedonian guards, who returned their fire, it said.
After several minutes of gunfire, the Albanian police fled, leaving weapons and equipment behind, the Ministry said.

The Macedonian Defence Ministry said the security situation along its border with Albania, in the region of the Ohrid and Prespa lakes, was deteriorating rapidly amid fresh reports of gunfire from light and heavy weapons across the border.

Macedonian Radio said there appeared to be complete chaos on that part of the border, with no regular army or police presence and no border controls. The rebels had seized and looted two border watchtowers, it said.

An Albanian officer told the radio station "there is chaos in Peshkopeja and two captured tanks are being driven through the town". People had looted 40 tonnes of wheat from the state reserves, he said.
Macedonian Radio reported that citizens of the border town Ohrid could hear gunfire from heavy and light artillery and see rockets flying above the lake.
Macedonia proclaimed its independence from former Yugoslavia in 1991.
Yugoslavia's top military body, the Supreme Defence Council, decided on Thursday to raise combat readiness of a part of the second and third armies in the region bordering with Albania.
The state border towards the republic of Albania is closed until further notice, the Yugoslav news agency Tanjug said.
Before the barriers went down, a column of vehicles which crossed onto Yugoslav territory included a dozen cars and jeeps with some 50 badly frightened Catholic priests and nuns.
"Not even during World War Two did monks and nuns leave their monasteries," one of them told local journalists.

The Yugoslav government, in its first official comment on the violence in Albania, said the "deep destabilisation ... with implications for the stability of the region is causing the federal government's concern." It called for a peaceful political settlement to the crisis.
Ethnic Albanians account for almost one-fifth of the 10-million population of Serbia which together with tiny Montenegro comprises new Yugoslavia.
